When, and only when, this rite has been completed will the dead heed the necromancer’s call and give the answers once hidden by the shroud of death.
Libre Necronomicon

There’s an ancient tale told in Ultherst of the conflict between Margrave Leopold of Calmariland and Wilhelm II of Ultherst. It’s said that in 508, Wilhelm II issued a writ to be handed to every citizen, from the lowliest swineherds to the loftiest nobles, informing them to gather up whatever weapon they could in preparation for the fight which was to come. In response, according to Herman the Chronicler, every peasant from Hillbrandt to Alvaron armed himself with a knife and made for the front, ready to die for their lord.\\n\\Knives are generally smaller than daggers, crafted with asymmetrical blades more useful for slashing than piercing. Larger knives are sometimes confused for sabers, though only an untrained fighter could mistake them in close quarters combat. Though often small and thought the weapons of assassins, more than a few lives have been saved, and taken, by the simplest of knives.
Knife

It's a severely decayed corpse—most likely that of a young girl. The body was found near the Dragon Rock at the place where in all likelihood a heretic mass must have taken place. The cadaver has been already fully affected by the putrefaction and bones are thus protruding at several places. The face was partially gnawed off by woodland beasts and the rotting flesh is crawling with larvae of various insects. The chest is open which suggests removal of the inner organs. With considerable certainty the corpse has been exposed to the effects of weather for several weeks already, which can be used to deduce the time of death.
Dead girl

This corpse, that of a young girl, is in a moderate state of decay. Judging from her overly distorted facial features, the poor darling was likely simple. A tear from sternum to umbilical suggests that something burst from her chest. The maggots have not yet grown fat from her flesh; her death was fairly recent.

This is the fresh corpse of what appears to have once been a young woman.  I found her remains in the dungeon beneath the Arch Bishop’s palace, where a heretical mass most likely took place. At most, the death occurred hours ago. Rigor Mortis has barely taken hold of her limbs, and the contortion of her facial muscles indicates that her death was utterly gruesome. The abdominal cavity is prolapsed and the womb is shredded... something appears to have hatched from within her body. God forgive me, I pray I never have to write those words ever again.

As the name suggests, two-handed swords are most often wielded with two hands, making the weapon more or less useless to a mounted warrior. The construction of two-handed swords usually follows a rather simple blueprint: a straight double-edged blade, which is usually fitted with quillons or flukes; a guard; a grip; and of a pommel. Due to the nature of the blades, two-handers are usually around the same length as their wielders. There are thus rare cases of two-handed swords reaching nearly seven feet in length, wielded by men who command the field like Titans. Because of their size, two-handed swords are carried without a scabbard either on the back with the hilt above the shoulder or with the blade resting on the arm.\\n\\nTwo-handed swords are a relatively new invention in terms of weaponry. First employed in the twelfth century, they were most often used to break breaches or to drive back pikemen. Few things intimidate a legion of battle-hardened troops like a regiment of men wielding blades as long as their bodies. To say the weapons command respect is a disgrace to the institution of fear.
Two-handed sword

Few sights inspire as much dread on the battlefield as that of an armored cavalryman wielding a two-handed flail. Most often constructed by attaching a weighted iron ball and chain to a sturdy shaft, these weapons wreak absolute havoc on ranks of infantrymen. Some variants, consisting of several smaller weights attached to multiple chains, literally whip enemy combatants into a fearful frenzy. These “Cat-o-nine-tails” variants are used most often by robber tyrants and sadistic marauders, men who can truly appreciate the scale of the destruction they sow.
Two-handed flail

Two-handed axes resemble their one-handed counterparts in nearly every way save length. In fact, they are nearly indistinguishable from their civilian counterpart, the common logging axe, to most untrained eyes. Unlike two-handed swords and double-blade axes, two-handed axes are incredibly easy to wield and require much less space than their more “elegant” contemporaries. Though similar in design to one-handed axes, and as easy to produce, two-handed axes bring a level of force to the battlefield rivaled only by the fury of Hell itself. The added length of the haft allows the weapon to generate more kinetic energy on each swing, easily severing unprotected limbs. Few men live to see things more terrifying than a berserker wielding a two-handed axe; fewer still live to appreciate them.
Two handed axe

Though no one can truly say who the hero is in the struggle between belts and belt loops, none can argue that belts have truly revolutionized fashion in the orthodox world. Adorned with gems or jewelry, they can be handsome accessories as well as war tools, easily holding the weight of a sword without failing in their original purpose. Belts, without a doubt, have forced us to hold our civilization (and our civilization’s pants) to a higher standard.
Belt

These are the grisly remains of Amelina von Blutenreich, the first wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich. They are all that was left of the poor creature after she was tortured to death in her husband’s unholy torture chambers. I can only imagine the horrors she must have endured. God rest her tormented soul.
Remains of Amelina von Blutenreich

These are the remains Miraquel von Blutenreich, the second wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich. Her tainted corpse was little more than skin and bones, and her face was a twisted vision of absolute agony. I pray her second death was more merciful than the first; no God-fearing being should ever suffer as she did. May she find peace and rest at the right hand of our Father.
Remains of Miraquel von Blutenreich

These are the remains of Betuana von Blutenreich, the third wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich. Even in a state of undeath, her youth is apparent. There is little question that she suffered terribly at his hands before finally succumbing. God rest her poor soul. I will see her death, and the deaths of the rest of von Blutenreich’s wives, avenged.
Remains of Betuana von Blutenreich

These are the remains of Sylviana von Blutenreich, the fourth wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich. From the look of her body, one could assume the Baron held a particular distaste for poor Sylviana. Her limbs are a gory mess, her face battered and bruised even before her second slaying. God, how could a man do this to the women he swore to love and cherish?
Remains of Sylviana von Blutenreich

These are the remains of Verra von Blutenreich, the fifth wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich. The poor creature, her rotten tongue and lips are curved as if trying to form the word “please.” She died once begging for her life, and again begging for true death.I... I cannot believe a man of flesh and blood could do this to a woman, let alone his own wife. How could no one have foreseen this after the death of four previous wives?
Remains of Verra von Blutenreich

These are the remains of Verena von Blutenreich, the sixth wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich. There’s barely anything left of her. Her limbs are wasted and frail, meaning she likely held out the longest of any of the Baron’s late wives. Her once beautiful hair was bloodied and matted to her face, hiding her visage in death. I granted her what peace I could. Lord, please comfort her in the next life.
Remains of Verena von Blutenreich

These are the remains of Almina von Blutenreich, the seventh wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich. Where the Baron’s other wives died full of fear or hopelessness, it is clear that Almina died full of hate. Her features are a mask of loathing, twisted and torn like some of the hellspawn I’ve come across in my travels. God, please have mercy on her, and bar her not from the gates of Heaven for her wrath. It was as well deserved as any.
Remains of Almina von Blutenreich

These are the remains of Ulpie von Blutenreich, the eighth wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich.What a curious name: Ulpie. It isn’t Ultherstian. The poor darling must have been a foreigner, but from where, I wonder?\\n\\nWhat horror it must have been, leaving behind your family and homeland to marry a foreign Baron, only to be kept in chains and starved to death. God, I can only imagine the things she must have felt in her final moments. Did she welcome death when it finally descended upon her? She did the second time. That much is clear. Never have I seen a revived corpse’s facial muscles relax so drastically after relinquishing undeath. If I didn’t know better, I’d say she tried to smile before her soul left its ruined husk. I hope that’s the case. Sleep well, little Ulpie.
Remains of Ulpie von Blutenreich

These are the remains of Deneara von Blutenreich, the ninth wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich. What sane world allows a man to marry nine times? What spell must he have held over the local gentry that no one wondered how every woman he married fell ill or disappeared? Deneara is much like the others: starved, beaten and tortured. She accepted her second death with grace, though the hate buried within her made her a significant threat to the living. Her husband, though? Hell may have been forged in earnest for beasts like the Dark Prince, but its halls will welcome von Blutenreich before this is all said and done. Mark my word.
Remains of Deneara von Blutenreich

These are the remains of Anna von Blutenreich, the tenth wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich. Ten women dead and for what? What has the Baron gained except a reputation for murder and state-sponsored adultery. Anna’s death, thankfully, seemed to be have more merciful than that of the Baron’s previous wives. She appears as though she wasted away from illness, quickly, judging from her undiminished, though not unsightly, mass. In undeath, she was a formidable opponent, but like the others she accepted her second ending. She rests now in the arms of her Lord.
Remains of Anna von Blutenreich

These are the remains of Nicoletta von Blutenreich, the eleventh wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich. Her body is in terrible shape. The Baron must have taken a shine to beating her, blotched and bloodied as he skin is. Eleven wives slain and yet more to count, all tortured and raised in death by the man they once loved. There can be no doubt: Von Blutenreich is viler than a great many of the demons in Hell.
Remains of Nicoletta von Blutenreich

These are the remains of Petriella von Blutenreich, the twelfth wife of Baron Dawn von Blutenreich. Thankfully, she will be the last risen wife I have to put to rest. Like the others, she fought with a rage known only to scorned women and the Furies themselves yet accepted death with a martyr’s grace. She sleeps now, nestled in the arms of her Lord. God, grant me the strength to bring them the justice they deserve.
Remains of Petriella von Blutenreich

This is a freshly slain sheep... and that’s really all there is to it. It looks to have been healthy at one time, aside from being dead, of course. I know a few recipes, but how would I go about making any of them? I don’t have an ounce of butter on me, and I’m not even sure how I’d go about making a decent polenta with the things in my travel pack. Alas, the road is no place for fine cuisine; why must this life be so cruel?
Dead sheep

Maces are sturdy blunt weapons formed by attaching an iron or steel “head,” usually in the shape of a ball or star, to a wooden shaft. Maces are extremely effective in close quarters, but are also sometimes used by cavalry. The amount of blunt force generated by a mounted warrior swinging a mace can sometimes be enough to sever the head of an unsuspecting victim, as grisly and gruesome as that is to imagine.
Mace

Few shields can match the pavise in terms of sheer protective power. Larger and sturdier than most other shields, the pavise’s only flaw is that it’s large size often feels clumsy in truly fluid combat scenarios. Perfect for deflecting arrows, however, the pavise has become the staple of organized units of warriors looking to protect not only themselves but also the men fighting at their side.
Pavise

These are Hazmidar seals, bound to the spirit of the demon for which they are named. Like all seals, they can be used to invoke the power of a fallen spirit, in this case, the Lord of Fire grants the user a simulated fireball spell. Seals, due to their mystical nature, cast regardless of their user’s Intelligence or ability to use magic.\\n\\nIn ages long past, Hazmidar was a pagan demon of fire, feared and revered the world over for his fiery temper and his equally burning lust. When his desires turned solely to Shauni, the pagan Goddess of Water, Hazmidar turned his fire on his fellows. Burning all of Shauni’s suitors to cinders, the bemused Goddess had little choice but to marry the demon who had striven so hard to win her heart. In the end, the consummation of their love was the death of Hazmidar, but many say he died with a smile. The church reminds us that lust is often rewarding to the senses, but will leave us as withered as any other sin in time; I’m sure Hazmidar would agree.
Hazmidar

Morath seals can be used to invoke the spirit of the fell dragon for which they are named. They grant their user a simulated fireball spell, capable of reducing even the toughest of foes to ashes. Seals, due to their mystical nature, cast regardless of their user’s Intelligence or ability to wield miracles.\\n\\nThe ancient Letmerians and the wily Dakens considered Morath, a terrible dragon of the Old World, to be the son of Odmar, the Allgod King. Pagans the world over feared him, believing that his fires could boil the seas and sear the flesh from bones, for so the dragon would have them believe.  Morath was eventually slain by a pagan chieftain, Beowulf, who unfortunately did not survive their encounter. The two died locked in bitter combat, neither of them any the wiser of their wounds, neither willing to admit they had been bested. Morathi famously said before death took the both of them, “you are no mouse, who fights like a lion.” To this, Beowulf responded, “I am no man, who fights like a dragon; I am Beowulf.” In the end, the church would remind us that giving in to selfish pride will be man’s downfall, for no matter how much we believe in ourselves, each of us might be brought low in such times by something as small as a mouse or so frightening as a dragon.
Morath

Goraphiel seals are bound the ancient Godsmith of the Erebornian pantheon. They grant their user a simulated firewall spell. Like all seals, this firewall be can conjured regardless of their user’s Intelligence or casting ability.\\n\\nGoraphiel was supposedly the greatest smith in all of creation, capable even, as the Erebornians would no doubt attest, that he could forge weapons which even God Almighty could not shatter. He carried his forge fires with him everywhere, capable of erecting a wall of flame that could sustain itself even in the kingdom of Shauni, the Sea Goddess. Goraphiel lived a long, but rather uneventful life, so far as the pagan gods are concerned. The church would remind us that no matter how hot one’s inner fire might burn, it is but a flash in the pan if never put to good use.
Goraphiel

Marchiel seals are consecrated in the name of Marchiel, Angel of Wrath, the close compatriot of Gabriel and his arch-angelic brethren. Like all seals, they may be used regardless of their user’s Intelligence and casting ability. These seals in particular grant their user the ability to hurl bolts of lightning.\\n\\nMarchiel is known by many as the Angel of Wrath, and with good reason. It was not uncommon, before the birth of the First Prophet, for holy men to invoke Marchiel’s name when they had been wronged by other members of the church, for so was the angel’s wrath that he would often strike betrayers dead with his lightning. Hungry for retribution, Marchiel treated every wayward sinner as if they were the Fallen Prince himself, longing for the day when he might lay low the Dark One. The church reminds us that Wrath unrestrained is a sin in itself, but when it is directed righteously at the enemies of God, the wrathful carry with them the strength and conviction of Marchiel, Lord of Thunder.
Marchiel

Azriah seals are consecrated in the name of the godling, Azriah, son of Odmar the Godking. These seals grant their user the ability to cast chain-lightning despite their Intelligence or casting ability.\\n\\nAzriah, the prankster god, was fond of riling his father. One of his favorite pastimes was shooting sheep. According to legend, Azriah would often spend hours in his father’s pastures, herding sheep only to electrocute them three at a time.
Azriah

Mirael seals are consecrated in the name of Mirael, the pagan Goddess of Thunder. These seals grant their user the ability to cast a living thunderstorm which follows the caster for a time. They can be used regardless of the caster’s Intelligence or innate casting ability.\\n\\nIn legend, Mirael was the sister of Shauni, Goddess of Water. She was initially relegated to govern the emotions of affection and love, but her fury won out in the end. When Odmar the Godking approached her with the crown of her godhood, she fought him off with bolts of lightning that rattled creation itself. Seeing her rage, Odmar promptly changed his mind. He left her the crown, though.
Mirael

Ziraliah seals grant their user the ability to hurl bolts of frost at his or her enemies. These seals are consecrated in the name of Ziraliah, chief among the giant tribes.\\n\\nZiraliah, as the mythos states, was the only giant capable of spitting frost. His freezing breath was said to have been able to shatter stone. It came as no surprise then that Ziraliah was at the head of the giant’s charge against the gods when their slight led to the Creation War. When the gods refused to invite the giants to their great feast, they stormed the temple where it was held and laid waste to the festivities. Ziraliah, or so the story goes, froze Odmar in his seat and would have killed him were it not for Azriah’s interference. Unfortunately, Odmar didn’t come away unscarred. He lost an eye in the ordeal – not to Ziraliah’s breath, but to his son’s lightning. Ziraliah laughed even as he and the rest of his kind fled, leaving a trail of shattered ice wherever his breath had condensed in the air.
Ziraliah

Vidergo seals are consecrated in the name of the Erebornian god, Vidergo the Terrible. They allow their user to cast an expanding ring of frost capable of chilling their foes to the bone.\\n\\nVidergo, a lonely god by all rights, entertained himself by performing all manner of evil deeds. His favorite activity involved coming down from the mountains by night to destroy the crops of farmers who refused to pray to him. Vidergo would sit in a field of ripening corn or wheat and channel his freezing powers until ever ear and every stalk was stone dead. In the morning, the farmers would wake to a field of dead crops, signed with the frozen rings of Vidergo’s loathing.
Vidergo

Elgaroth seals are consecrated in the name of Elgaroth, the cunning lord of goblins. They grant their user the ability to cast bolts of frost which slow and damage their enemies.\\n\\nElgaroth, a cunning prince among goblinkind, decided one day that he had had quite enough of the gods’ tampering in the lives of mortals. One cool morning, he challenged the gods to a footrace, claiming he could beat the strongest and fastest of them with ease. Never to be outdone, the gods accepted. When the race began, Elgaroth turned and froze the gods where they stood. Unable to move without the aid of Goraphiel’s fire (as Goraphiel had neglected to come to the race, convinced by the other gods that he was too slow and clumsy), the remaining gods watched in anger as Elgaroth strutted to the finish line.
Elgaroth

Pearls are widely recognized as the diamonds of the sea, found only within the shells of strange beings known only as “oysters.” Though they are now believed to form as calcium deposits within the oyster’s shell, many pagan cultures believed that pearls were rewards from Shauni, Goddess of Water, bestowed upon mortals who sang beautiful songs to her. Pearl divers would often form choirs, singing their praise to the seal, before diving in search of the sea’s bounty.
Pearl

Bucklers, sometimes called “punching shields,” are generally small, round implements used to deflect dagger blows. Usually made of metal, these little shields are most often used for blade dueling. Their size and weight make them impractical for true hand-to-hand combat, where a mace or axe might shatter bones in the wrist.
Buckler

Pikes are thrusting polearms most often used to reduce the effectiveness of mounted warriors and armored knights. They were first introduced to the battlefield in the 11th century when Erstwick Landsknechts made use of the weapon in three separate Crusades. Watching their armies fall prey to men with “simple spears” time and time again, the lords of the faithful world soon realized that these polearms might hold some merit as weapons after all.
Pike

This strange parchment was found among the personal belongings of the late Judge Vallarian. Judging from the thickness, the parchment is most likely made of human skin. That fact alone is terrifying enough, but the ancient language scrawled across its surface distresses me further. Perhaps if I could translate it, it might help me to better understand the fallen judge’s ambitions.\\n\\nAs written, it reads:\\n\\nEn Orthaxx Nefreth Balduin Cosmisane Turbiculum Jahved Somiell Ukkzahb Haabruk Desmisorxx Afthromid Rocibus Sancturis Pergmoth Eezghrebb Honved Umbria Poisuan Reisatg Ulbrefiel Hanthoss Benedictus Eredicum Syfilium Aesmeziel Ptorax Treptemon Yloath Eb Mosiel Ad Trufixis Dosmosis Loatrium Ghorbell Kpterax Oermis Doe Si Ulmoarth Sine Qua Non Gervais Edudand Franzimor Sobres Kusth Erbis Erebis Dorum Qertmorth Dorr.
Strange human skin parchment

This shred of a richly embroidered cloak was found in a thorny bush in the Glatzburg cemetery. No doubt it belongs to the defiler of a nearby grave. A piece of clothing is direct evidence... more than enough for a conviction.
Shred of a cloak

A classical suit of plate armor consists of several interlocking pieces, namely: a cuirass having breast and back plates; a gorget; pauldrons; a tasse; culets; fauld; and a chainmail skirt. When assembled correctly and worn over chainmail, a full suit of plate armor is second only to the love of God in terms of its protective value.
Plate armor

This strange parchment was among Judge Vallarian’s possessions. Made from human skin and etched in an ancient language, the secrets it holds could be crucial to understanding what the fallen judge’s sinister intentions were.\\n\\nThe translation, provided by Wisewoman Enrie Jungwirdt, reads:\\n\\nOn the Eve of Damned Balduin\\nNine years after the Night without Wood\\nThe Four Messages intact with Seals\\nFor the men in Red Robes\\nFor the traitors of Umbria\\nTo the land of No Man where no stakes burned\\n\\nEach Twenty and One years after the Damned Balduin\\nNine successive followers\\nThis is the Plan\\n\\nIn the crypt of pagans who saw the Light\\n\\nThe Last will meet and then go in Three Directions\\n\\nInto the Shadow of a Dragon the First will step\\n\\nThe Second shall go where the Denhelitians once danced\\n\\nAnd the Third must find Satan’s Maw\\n\\nThe prison shall be opened, and vengeance will come.

Conceivably, anything that could be worn about the head to provide protection to its wearer could be considered a helmet. Though helmets provide a modest amount of security to their wearer in the midst of combat, many find that wearing one allows them to focus more on the task at hand. Capable of deflecting arrows, some stronger helmets, most often made of plate, are stylized in the fashion of animals or mythical beasts, and are meant to inspire dread in their wearer’s enemies. The helmets of rank and file soldiers, however, are often simple and, as many soldiers would agree, utterly useless when it comes to staving off an incoming axe or hammer blow.
Helmet

This golden ring is much like any other - a simple piece of finery worked around a beautiful gem. However, in one way, this ring is utterly unique. It bears an enchantment, though holy or unholy none could say without further inspection. Therefore, one must always take care when handling or wearing such jewelry. A wise man always waits to get a jeweler’s opinion on such things before risking life and limb to look just a touch more dashing.
Ring

The name “Guss Halworth” is engraved into the inner lining of this absolutely gorgeous ring. Made of solid gold and set with a diamond as big as my thumb, it would easily fetch a price at market that would likely make even the king wince to hear it.
Halworth's ring

This ring once belonged to the late Archbishop Martroiani, who oversaw the Holy Mother Church before the ascension of Archbishop Laurencius. The circumstances of his death are mysterious, to say the least.\\n\\nThe ring is massive, made of pure gold and adorned with a giant ruby - a symbol of the Archbishop's cathedral. A portion of the Book of Necra - tenth book of the Holy Scriptures - engraved into the inner side of the ring.
Bishop Martroiani's ring

This coffin contains the remains of Baron Liam von Hunth. It’s little more than an oaken box, indicating that not even the von Hunths were spared from the Scourges. A sad sight indeed when even noble houses can scarcely afford to bury their dead.
Coffin of Baron von Hunth

Composite bows, first used in the conflict between Ereborn and Endarion in the fifth century A.E., consist of a wooden core, a layer of horn on the belly and of multiple (sometimes even eight) layers of sinew on the back. As any bowyer would proudly tell you, the entire construct is held together by sinew and bone glue alone. Due to the demanding nature of their construction, composite bows are often smaller than regular bows. Their fine construction, however, allows them to shoot much farther.
Composite bow

Ahalaar's Will. The name alone was enough to strike fear into the hearts of men returning from the Holy Wars, and with good reason.\\n\\nThe Jad-Habaal have long been famous for their peculiar fighting style. Making great use of curved swords and cloth armor, the Jad-Habaal are perhaps most famous for their mounted archers; fearless warriors wielding short bows who ride wild desert stallions into battle. Of these warriors, none was more feared than Shaik Omhar Bhutaar ad Kandahaar, a noble of the third era known to his foes only as “Dead Shot.” With his bow, Ahalaar’s Will, which was said to be able to strike a faithless man dead in the eye from over two-hundred meters away, he laid waste to his enemies of his heathen god.\\n\\nThe bow’s creation was commissioned for use in the Holy War declared in 385 by King Rafmaanii the Wise of Kandahaar. The relic fell into the hands of the faithful during the Second Crusade by members of the Order of the Holy Cross, who looted it from the corpse of a nameless pagan general. How that general came to possess such a marvelous weapon, none would ever learn, but the bow remained in the Order’s possession until 1211 when it was given to the Grand Master of the Brotherhood of the Righteous, Pierre de Lemroix, for his aid in the defense of Jevaran. It was brought to Ultherst soon after.
Ahalaar's Will

This suit of armor was worn by the Archangel Gabriel himself, if some legends are to be believed. Supposedly the Emissary of the Lord gave it to the prophet, King David II of Ultherst in the year 999 to aid him in defending the Realm from a demonic incursion prophesied to occur at the turn of the millennium. The invasion never took place, but the armor remained in the possession of the ruling house of Ultherst and was worn in many battles through the Hundred Years War and multiple crusades. Rumor has it that the famous explorer Raymond Flayerd, who conquered the primitive empire of Azthallax, wore the armor in his holy conquest of the New World.
Angelic Armor

This ring, made of pure gold and brimming with enchantments, was named in honor, or perhaps in spite of, Jean Baptiste II, the Pope who guided the Church during the Schism.\\n\\nAt the forefront of the Hundred Years War was the Schism, a conflict that would forever reshape the religious landscape of the Orthodox world. When Calmariland waged war with the Empire, Jean Baptiste II spoke out, denouncing the Empire’s neighbor and former ally. Baptiste ordered Ingnatius I, the Archdiocese of Calmariland, to convince his king and noble countrymen to lay down their arms and present themselves before the Church to be judged. Unwilling to follow the orders of a now foreign Pope, Ignatius spurned the orders and was ordered himself to appear before the golden throne of Baptiste. Ignatius refused once again. In a fit of anger, Ignatius declared himself the head of the Church of Calmariland and renounced all claim of the Holy Mother over his homeland. To seal his new position, he had a golden ring handcrafted for the office of Archbishop of Calmariland that bore a striking resemblance to the papal mark. When he learned of its existence, Church scholars claim that Jean Baptiste flew into a rage that never truly ceased, from whence the ring eventually took its name.
Baptiste's Rage

This mighty relic owes its fame to Joachym of Vincezzi, one of the first papal inquisitors to wear it.\\n\\nJoachym de Vincezzi was named Supreme Inquisitor of Rhie and Whelminster in 1161. It was a time of great civil strife and the Church laid waste to several villages and cities in its zeal. From 1161 to 1172, over 20,000 people were accused of heresy. Among their number were pregnant mothers and small children. Despite numerous discussions regarding the lawfulness his drastic methods and the guilt of the accused, none can deny that Joachym of Vincezzi did kill his fair share of heretics and godless creatures. Several inquisitors and Church tribunals have since followed Joacyhm’s example, and for a time after his passing, torches and stakes were as common as rain in Lochland.n\\nDespite the supposed good Joachym’s work did, it’s worth noting that his actions eventually led to the rebellion of Koliash of Montharth. Before succumbing to death, Koliash claimed that the “Scourge of God” had driven him to his bloody vengeance. Historians at the time believed that Koliash’s statement was meant to represent the symbol of Joachym’s ring, which had become a banner for inquisitorial work the world over.
Scourge of God

Saint Baudolino has been the subject of countless discussions in the Church throughout the years. Many religious scholars challenge whether or not the man ever existed to begin with.\\n\\nRegardless of where the truth really lies, there are many relics, real and fabricated, which have been ascribed to Saint Baudolino over the course of centuries. Of these, perhaps none are more famous than The Boots of Saint Baudolino, which he supposedly wore in the gardens of the Palace of Ekriptides. According to legend, the boots gained their magical powers when Baudolino (rather fuddled at the time) waded through the sacred river Kunqa which no one, with the exception of Priest John himself, was allowed to enter. The trespass, of course, was punished with banishment. As Saint Baudolino boarded the Divine Voyager to return home, Priest John gifted him with ten carafes of wine – a friendly parting gift, despite the rift which had grown between them. Baudolino accepted the wine and drunk heavily on his journey home, blissfully unaware that the enchantments placed upon the drink would wipe his memory clean. Thus, Saint Baudolino and his men never divulged the location of Ekriptides, the land of Priest John, and the famous gardens were lost for an age.
Boots of Saint Baudolino

When the Landsknechts of Erstwick defeated the Crusade sent against them in the year 999, the faithful took notice first of their courage. Then, as the shock of defeat slowly wore off, the faithful began to take notice of their enemies’ weapon – the mighty polearm. Of these strange new polearms, the strongest by far was the legendary Dies Irae, meaning“Wrath of God” in Old Lateran.\\n\\nDies Irae was the weapon of choice forCommander Koliash of Montharth—dreaded leader of the populist rebellion in Lochland in 1165. The revolt was the direct result of the mass executions handed down by the papal inquisition in the provinces of Rhie and Whelminster, many at the behest of Joachym of Vincezzi. Commander Koliash took his place as the leader of the popular rebellion and led the people to several victories over both Lochland armies and Crusaders. He used his feared halberd both mounted and on the ground, sowing death into the ranks of his enemies as if he was a reaper cutting wheat. The halberd was imbued with many magic powers thanks to the blessing of Bishop Angelius of Montharth who was a stalwart supporter of Commander Koliash.\\n\\nIn the end the revolt was quenched in blood due to a betrayal and Koliash himself died in the Battle of Khiell—his halberd was then taken to Ultherst as the Ultherst nobles were the first to seize the Commander's legendary weapon after his unfortunate demise.
Dies Irae

Dragon mantle is a cursed relic made by the Dark Prophet Aahmaton from the skin of the last dragon slain in the Old World. Dragons were the creation of the Beast, offspring of the Dark Lord and the earthly emissaries of the fallen angels. They caused havoc wherever they roamed, slaughtering all the living and taking all the treasures, then they retreated into deep abysses and murky caverns to sleep on the hoarded treasures, resting before they decided to go pillaging again. Many great Saints were dedicated to killing those monsters, among others Saint George, whose lance was blessed for the purpose by the Archangel Gabriel himself.\\n\\nDragon Mantle is made of gold, silver and steel dragon scales which makes it almost impenetrable by ordinary weapons. It gained the magic properties from the dark powers that kept the dragon alive for many millennia.
Dragon Mantle

Dragon Talon was one of the many relics taken from the grasp of the pagan realm of Jad-Habaal during the First Crusade, which has so far actually been the only successful Crusade undertaken—the crusaders were able to conquer Jevaran and free the Holy Grave, although only for a short time. Dragon Talon was probably used in pagan rituals as a sacrificial dagger, nevertheless it can be used in melee combat as well. Each time either of its two blade tastes blood the red rubies on the hilt of the mystical weapon begin to glow.
Dragon Talon

It was in the year 951 when Ulthar the Terrible, the Chieftain of the clan of Hanths of the Icy plains, embarked on his gruesome campaign across the face of the Faithful World. He thus unleashed the conflict which is nowadays known as the Barbarian Wars. The legends describe him as a being of superhuman strength which is not surprising considering the fact that his mother was the famous immortal giantess Morthulla. That's why he was able to wield the war axe dubbed Skull Crusher which was made of unknown unimaginably heavy metal. Wielding his axe, made and enchanted by Morthulla herself, Ulthar the Terrible breached the borders of all the Faithful Kingdoms of the Old World, crushed their resistance and enslaved them in terrible pagan darkness. The rumor was that as long as he wielded his weapon he could not be defeated by any adversary. Nevertheless death came to him from an unexpected direction—he was murdered in his sleep by his own brother who wanted to become the Chieftain of the clan. Besides Ulthar's life he took his axe as well. Nevertheless it was too heavy for him and during the Battle of Fiondland Marshes it dragged him down to the bottom of a bog.
Skull Crusher

According to legend, Queen Penelope of Calmariland ordered this famous short sword’s construction for her lover, Raymond Flayerd, a renowned explorer and the discoverer of the New World, on the occasion of his embarking on a voyage to prove the existence of lands other than those of the Old World. Even though Raymond Flayerd was born as an Ultherst Squire, he spent all his life seeking the mysterious lands to be found somewhere across the ocean. Nevertheless his wanderlust was not looked upon too kindly in Ultherst—on the contrary the Inquisition became interested in his views of the world and thus he left for the more liberal Calmariland where he soon became well known at the royal court thanks to his adventurous deeds. It was there that he met Penelope, the wife to Carlos I. It didn't take them long to become lovers. When he was leaving on his famous voyage in 1208, the Queen of Calmariland ordered the creation of a rare sword which was to protect him from all perils lurking across the Great Ocean. The sword acquired its name, which means The Conqueror in the language of Calmariland, after the second and the third voyage to the New World during which Raymond Flayerd crushed a native kingdom named Azthallax.\\n\\nFlayerd was accused of heresy by the Papal Inquisition in 1215 as the Holy Mother Church could not suffer its dogmatic teaching regarding the immutable structure of the Kingdom of God on Earth to be contravened. Thanks to Flayerd's relatives the sword came back to Ultherst after the explorer's execution. Unfortunately the sword got lost after 1219 and there have been only rumors ever since.
El Conquistador

According to legend, Queen Penelope of Calmariland ordered this famous leather surcoat to be made for her lover Raymond Flayerd, a renowned explorer and the discoverer of the New World, on the occasion of his embarking on a voyage to prove the existence of lands other than those of the Old World. Even though Raymond Flayerd was born as an Ultherst Squire, he spent all his life seeking the mysterious lands to be found somewhere across the ocean. Nevertheless his wanderlust was not looked upon too kindly in Ultherst—on the contrary the Inquisition became interested in his views of the world and thus he left for the more liberal Calmariland where he soon became well known at the royal court thanks to his adventurous deeds. It was there that he met Penelope, the wife to Carlos I It didn't take them long to become lovers. When he was leaving on his famous voyage in 1208, the Queen of Calmariland ordered the creation of an excellent suit of leather armor which was to protect him from all perils lurking across the Great Ocean. The armor acquired its name, which means The Protector in the language of Calmariland, after the second and the third voyage to the New World during which Raymond Flayerd crushed a native kingdom named Azthallax—the armor saved Flayerd's life several times.\\n\\nFlayerd was accused of heresy by the Papal Inquisition in 1215 as the Holy Mother Church could not suffer its dogmatic teaching regarding the immutable structure of the Kingdom of God on Earth to be contravened. Thanks to Flayerd's relatives the surcoat came back to Ultherst after the explorer's execution. Unfortunately the surcoat got lost after 1219 and there have been only rumors ever since.
El Protector

According to legend, Queen Penelope of Calmariland commissioned this famous pair of enchanted gloves for her lover, Raymond Flayerd, a renowned explorer and the discoverer of the New World, on the eve before his journey to the new world. Though Raymond Flayerd had been born an Ultherstian Squire, he spent most of his life plumbing the depths of far continents in search of power and glory. Nevertheless, his wanderlust was not regardedfavorably in Ultherst—on the contrary, the Inquisition took great interest in his views of the world, forcing Flayerd to seek shelter in the more-liberal state of Calmariland. It was there, having been invited to court for his many storied deeds, that Flayerd met Penelope, the wife of Carlos I.\\n\\nThe two fell madly in love, escaping at every chance to bask in one another’s company. In 1208, before Flayerd set sail to conquer the West, Penelope had a pair of exquisite leather gloves made for her globe-trotting beau. The gloves acquired their name, which translates to “The Usurper” in the language of Calmariland, seemingly in reference to Flayerd’s conquering of Azthallax. Others believe the name was meant to imply that Flayerd had usurped Carlos’ place as Penelope’s king, if only in spirit.\\n\\nWhen news of his travels to the world began to spread like plague across the old one, Flayerd was accused of heresy by the Papal Inquisition. Flayerd’s family kept his magnificent gloves –along with the rest of his conqueror’s garb – after his untimely execution in 1215. Unfortunately the gloves were lost after 1219, their since having becoming a topic of great speculation and superstition.
El Usurpador

In the nameless depths of the past, when the world was ruled by pagan and non-human races, a terrible conflict came to pass—a conflict remembered simply as the Pagan Wars.\\n\\nIn the year 508 of the Old Era, a lengthy and bloody war of attrition between the stocky Erebornians and the mysterious, forest-dwelling Elenians began. The Erebornians, an industrious, war-mongering race, were ill content with their dainty, tree-loving neighbors. The Elenians, in spite of their short-tempered neighbors, lived in total harmony with nature, which they worshipped as a singular Goddess – the wellspring from which druidic magic ebbed.\\n\\nGallius Cerbius, a General of the Erebornian Republic Army and chosen of the Senate, knew the only way to break his enemy was to deprive the Elenians of their sacred druidic guardians. His plan was as simple as it was brilliant—if Cerbius could strip the Elenians of their sacred groves, their druid protectors would be powerless to stop an all-out Erebornian assault.\\n\\n Gallius Cerbius ordered master smiths to forge a mighty axe for that very purpose. When it was completed, he ordered the priests of Daaron, the highest god of the Erebornian Pantheon, to imbue the weapon with powerful enchantments. Gallius Cerbius used the axe, dubbed Endarian’s Bane, saw the destruction of countless Elenian trees and souls. After Gallius’ death, the axe became a symbol passed from one Supreme Republic General to another—until 396 when General Octavianus Sulpius used it to conquer the Elenian capital of Antheas. Not satisfied with anything less than ultimate victory, Octavianus departed for the Filkland Peninsula, where the last remnants of the Elenian people fled following the fall of their capitol. During one of the campaigns, Octavianus mysteriously disappeared and his famous axe with him. The Erebornians regarded his disappearance as an omen, and vowed from then on to respect their honored enemies in defeat.
Endarian’s Bane

When the Erstwick Crusade began, King Luther quickly realized his lightly armored militias would do little but die gracelessly in a akirmishwith the heavy cavalry of his enemies. According to legend, in one of Luther’s many fear-induced fever dreams, he met the angel Raphael, who advised him to journey to a forlorn fishing village on the shores of the Northern Sea. There, the angel claimed, Luther would find his people’s salvation.\n\\n When Luther arrived, he found little of use. The town was little more than a gathering of shanties, fallen into disrepair. As he prepared to leave, hopeless and broken, he saw fishermen spearing fish off the coast with long, wicked spears. The realization struck immediately. Luther ordered thousands of the specially-crafted spears for his armies—weapons that would soon be known as “pikes” for the town in which he’d found them, “Pike’s Landing.\\n\\nAt first, there were doubts about the efficiency of the new weapons among his men, and after a time, Luther feared they would refuse them in favor of more traditional swords and axes. Understanding that his men would never trust a spear in the command of a sword-wielding king, Luther had his own pike made. Beautiful and deadly, he had the weapon blessed by John Herman II, the Patriarch of the reformed Church of the True Word. At the behest of his men, Luther named the weapon the “Spike of Erstwick.”\\n\\n When the sun rose on the dawn of the first battle of the Erstwick Crusades, Luther hefted his pike and led his men with a cry and prayer into a veritable horde of marauding crusaders. Faced with the enemy’s heavy cavalry, Luther conquered unquestionably, dominating the field inboth Sadron and Meinheim. Horsemen the world over soon learned to fear the warrior king with the ten-foot reach. Luther’s name, and the name of his weapon, spread like wildfire across the civilized orld.\\n\\nThe Spike of Erstwick remained in the possession of Erstwick’s Kings until 1210, when it was stripped from the fallen king Darmont I. Though Erstwick won the war, the Ultherstians claimed the Spike of Erstwick as a spoil of war. It has remained in Ultherst ever since, longing to feel again Luther’s touch and the succulent warmth of horseflesh.
The Spike of Erstwick

Few angels hold the same level of esteem as Gabriel, the emissary. According to legend, it was he who saved the life of Friedrich the Brave, King of Lochland, at the Battle of Kunth in the year 411.//n//n The Battle of Kunth was the culmination of treason by Lochland’s Northern nobles against the Imperial Crown. Unsatisfied with Friedrich’s rule, the Northern lords vowed to take Lochland by force, threatening to break the nation into several small holdings if necessary. The royalists and separatists clashed near a small village named Kunth, where Friedrich soon found himself surrounded by the vastly superior numbers of unionist armies.\\n\\nWith a will of stone and the heart of a conqueror, Friedrich led a counterattack againstGrand Duke Vittorio the Hollander, the leader of the Northern Separation Union. In the end the savage duel ended with the Friedrich's victory—according to legends he owed that to the Archangel Gabriel who used a blessed, angelic shield to block several fatal blows from Vittorio. The rumor is that after the battle, Friedrich fell to his knees and prayed to Gabriel for delivering the battle to the righteous. Never far from the field, the Archangel heard his plea and appeared to bestow upon him a shield which would serve the leaders of Lochland for centuries. The Empire of Lochland, which has always been a firm bastion of the True Faith, has since made the shield a part of their very culture.\\n\\n The shield remained in the Imperial Armory until 1145 when it was given to King Joachym XII of Ultherst for his lending his aid in the Second Crusade. The shield has belonged to Ultherst ever since.
Gabriel's Shield

Few men have and ever will live up to the legend of Pontheus, wielder of Gladius Maximus, the blade which tamed the Galibornium Coliseum. Even though he was just a slave, Pontheus the slayer became would go on ot become more famous than any of his contemporaries, perhaps with the exception of Emperor Constantine, the Erebornian ruler who was overthrown by the armies of the faithful.\\n\\nPontheus's sword was most likely created by the priests and theurgists of the Cult of the Creators,who made their residences in the dungeons beneath the Coliseum. There, they worked ceaselessly turning hapless creatures and slaves into fearsome monsters fit for Pontheus’ blade. Audiences thousands strong packed the Coliseum day after day to watch the slayer fight, and day after day they were amazed by his cunning and brutality.\\n\\n After Galibornium was conquered by the army of Saint Orthenius, the Coliseum’s entrance was sealed and all of its inhabitants were left there to meet a gruesome end. It should be noted that, years later, when the gates were reopened, the body of Pontheus was not among the dead.
Gladius Maximus

There is no detailed information regarding the origin of this longbow. The relic was found at an ancient Elenian burial site which was discovered in 1145 in Ultherst—exactly in the tors near a town named Glen Moherr. The bow received its name after the place where it was found. Local Baron Harmond, who was obsessed with finding remnants of the Elenian settlements in Ultherst, was the one to find it. He was able to guess from the writings at the burial site that defiling the graves would be a terrible sacrilege bringing an eternal curse upon his head, but he decided to dig the graves anyway. In one of them he found a powerful bow which probably belonged to an Elenian noble. It was not proven whether the curse worked or if it was an accident, but Baron Harmond, together with the precious bow, disappeared soon after the discovery and nobody has heard about them since.
Glen Moherr Curse

Snake Fang, otherwise known as Kingbiter, is a relic of some renown. It was supposedly crafted by the vile queen, Eleanor, wife of Ulprecht, one of Ultherst’s first kings. Unbeknownst to Ulprecht at the time, he had married a snake-lover - a member of the cult of Slaanaar, the snake god. Though the dagger was originally used solely for ritual purposes, it is said that Eleanor wet the blade with the blood of her enemies many, many times.\\n\\nThe mad queen’s rampage lasted for years, claiming the lives of dozens of hapless noble lords and ladies. Her wicked reign of terror was at last ended by her husband, who caught her in the act just as she was attempting to murder the Bishop of Alvaron. Unfortunately, Ulprecht lacked the strength to sentence his beloved wife to death for her crimes, and banished her instead to live out the rest of her days in the lake-encircled castle of Ranoch. Nevertheless, the mad queen managed to escape her prison and vanish into the deep woods of the Northern Ultherst. There, some say, she reigns to this day, a wicked, half-human Queen of Slaanaar. The likeliest conclusion, however, is that the mad queen died in self-imposed exile, and that her dagger wound up in the hands of heretic cultists who continue her legend as a means of controlling the frightened northlands.
Snake Fang

Few can deny that Saint Jillian the Blessed was a man of many wonders, for few knew that he ever lived. Having been a hermit most of his life, Saint Jillian kept watch over the Moonshine Mountains as a humble sage. There he received travelers and pilgrims who sought him for his supposedly otherworldly wisdom, and wise he was, if the stories are true. So great and wise was he, in fact, that when the barbarian hordes descended from the North in 951, the Archangel Gabriel approached him with a single, divine request.\\n\\n“Lead the armies of the faithful, Sage Jillian, and bring glory to God’s kingdom,” the angel said, full of holy fire. His words would live on forever, etched into the gift he bestowed upon Saint Jillian for his promise: a helmet of tremendous power.\\n\\nIt is unclear whether the helmet gave Jillian his incredible strength, or whether it was buried within him all along, but what is known is that the hermit sage, already old when the war began, strode the battlefield like a vengeful god for thirty-eight years while wearing Gabriel’s gift.\\n\\nWhen the barbarians were finally driven out in 989, weary and with the name of the Divine Sage on their frightened lips, Saint Jillian laid down his arms and returned to his home. On a lonely road in the Moonshine Mountains, Saint Jillian was ambushed and violently stabbed to death by a band of roving tribeless – barbarians with no home left to return to. They destroyed the saint’s body in their hate-filled fury, and his glorious helmet, marked by Gabriel’s words, was lost for a time. Few alive remember the great Saint Jillian, but the phrase spawned from his passing passes many lips to this day; whenever a great man falls into unexpected trouble, the people of Ultherst say he was as prepared as a Moonshine Sage.
The Helm of Saint Jillian

No other weapon in all of Ultherst draws more reverence than Inquisitor, the blessed blade of Saint Orthenius.\\n\\nForged in the fires of creation, some say the blade was made for Orthenius thousands of years before his birth. They say the Lord cast it from the Arches of Heaven to cool, and that when He threw the blade to the Earth, he called out a battlecry to guide it into Saint Orthenius’waiting hands. The very same charge is inscribed along the weapon’s hilt: “Be righteous, Son of Man, forevermore.” And so his servant was, righteous and blessed by the Lord for all his days till death.\\n\\nBathed in arcing flame, the Inquisitor was said to be able to shear heads from necks with the ease of a reaper’s scythe passing through stalks of wheat. But, lo, the weapon was not only a slayer of men. When the city of Galiborneum refused to submit to his will, Saint Orthenius is said to have battered down the four-foot thick iron gates of the city with three terrible swings. God’s Judgment followed him swiftly into the pagan city, turning everything and everyone the blade struck into ash. Glory be to those who witnessed the Lord’s work, done by the hands of a man.\\n\\nAfter Saint Orthenius’ passing, Inquisitor was buried alongside him in a specially crafted tomb. There it rests in darkness to this day, forever reciting the holy name of God, lying in wait for a new Defender of the True Faith to rise and claim it.\\n\\nThat day, at last, has come.

Few weapons garner as much reverence as the Bane of Jad-Habaal, the fabled hammer of Wilhelm XI the Holy, King of Ultherst during the Crusades. Crusaders returning home from the Promised Land told fanciful stories of the hammer’s might, many claiming that the weapon was never sheathed bloodless. Rumor has it that Wilhelm XI used it to kill Sheikh Allhmaanii himself at the battle for the Jevaran Gate, shattering the ancient stone portal to pieces in the process. Historical sources credit Maxmilian II, the Emperor of Lochland, with the Sheikh’s death, however, regardless of who killed Allhmaanii, Jad-Habaal’s Bane became a symbol of power for the Crusaders who made it home alive. Wilhelm XI wielded it until his death, and it was thought to have been passed through his line. How it wound up here is a mystery...
The Bane of Jad-Habaal

Lizard Claw is an ancient artifact formerly belonging to Lord Zarg, the unclean ruler of the lizard people who made their home in the Devil’s Cavern, not far from the ruins of Galibornium. It’s impossible to say who made the thing, as old as it is. Some people seem to think the Devil’s Caverns are a gateway to Hell, and that the relic was made by Satan himself. Regardless of whether or not that’s true, the people of Glatzburg treat it as gospel, shooting down any ‘foolish’ notions that the lizardmen might actually be intelligent enough to forge their own steel.
Lizard Claw

If barbarian legends can be trusted, the Thunderbolt Hammer once belonged to a demon by the name of ‘Bhelfelix,’ whom the pagans of the Icy Plains once worshipped as a god. The pagan stories claim Bhelfelix forged the weapon himself as a gift for his most capable champion. When the Barbarian Wars started in 951 and the people of the Icy Plains eventually breached the borders of the Faithful World, it was High Priest Khurb-Athar who led his people to bloody conquest in Ultherst. Wielding the Thunderbolt Hammer beneath the banner of his Demon god, Khurb was a terror in the north for some time. Nevertheless, not even the mighty relic could save Khurb-Athar from utter defeat. When he fell in combat, the fleeing remnants of his army buried the relic together with a great treasure in the foothills of the Moonshine Mountains to prevent it from falling into the hands of the faithful. Not the best plan, in hindsight.
Thunderbolt Hammer

According to scripture, the man who would eventually become Saint George belonged to a rich family living in Cappadocia, the easternmost province of the Erebornian Empire. He served in the army of Emperor Diocletianus as an officer, accompanying the Emperor on his journey through the province. It seemed at one point that a promising future lay before the young officer. At a young age, his name was already known to perhaps the most powerful man in the world. All that changed, however in 118, when George accepted the True Faith and was mercilessly tortured to death for his beliefs.\\n\\n According to another legend, Saint George embraced the True Faith after he met a vicious dragon on some far flung battlefield. The ultimate incarnation of the beast, George fought for hours before the beast was slain, and only then because Gabriel himself had blessed the tip of his lance.\\n\\nRegardless of when George turned to the faith, the blessed lance was a thing of truth. It was lost after the Saint's death, but was found again during the First Crusade. Bearing the might of The Emissary himself, the lance became a symbol for the liberators of the Holy Grave. After the battle of Nashamir Fields, where the Crusaders suffered a terrible defeat at the hands of Omar II, the lance came into the possession of Aerin de Gublaire, a commander of the Brotherhood of the Righteous. When the crusaders returned from the Holy Lands, Gublaire brought the precious relic with him. It has remained in the Realm ever since.
Saint George's Lance

Blood Moon, the saber that might have killed a faith had the righteous not intervened. Blood Moon is a short saber that was first brought to the Realm by a band of Crusaders returning from the First Crusade. The weapon, forged from the finest Jad-Habaalian steel and bathed in he blood of countless righteous souls, was powerful with foreign, pagan enchantments. Blood Moon was looted from the Jevaran mosque of the Holy Prophet, and would eventually become the symbol of the aptly named Blood Moon Cult. Though the cult’s membership was a closely guarded secret, their goal was to ultimately destroy the True Faith and to replace it with the worship of Ahalaar, the god of Jad-Habaal.\\n\\n None can say how close the cult came to accomplishing their goal, but common knowledge is that their order was shattered by Giordanno de Loisson, Commander of the Brotherhood of the Righteous, wielding his fabled sword, Decapitator. Though the blood-slicked steel and Jad-Habaalian runes made the Blood Moon a formidable weapon, they could do little to augment its wielder. Decapitator took the fight with ease, living up to its name. Blood Moon, by virtue of its master’s defeat, lived up to its, as well.
Blood Moon

Glaives have been an integral part of warfare since 999, when the Erstwick Landsknechts under the command of King Luther drove off the Empire’s Crusaders with little more than their newly-adopted pikes. Similarly to Dies Irae, the relic of Commander Koliash of Monthart, which popularized the use of the halberd, Blood Bane was the relic that made glaives known throughout the faithful world.\\n\\nBlood Bane belonged to Philip of Kunttenburg, an infamous brigand and feared cutthroat descended from a noble Lochland family. Rumor has it that he partook in the Crusade against Erstwick in 999 to make amends for his sinful life—and almost found himself impaled on the end of a pike in a brutal counterattack that left many of his fellows dead. After the brush with death, Phillip decided to modernize arsenal and ordered a powerful glaive be made. After its completion, he had it enchanted by a monk named Gaspar, who was later accused of summoning of devils by the Papal Inquisition.\\n\\n Unaware of the dark enchantments tainting his weapon, Phillip found glory not on the battlefield, but along the royal roads, haunting villages and small towns with a roving army of brigans. His miserable life was ended in the Second Crusade against Erstwick, where once again, to atone for his sins, he was allowed to ride alongside the Crusaders. He was impaled by several pikes in a fruitless charge, and bled to death within minutes, or so the legend goes. After his death, Blood Bane was seized by the Ultherstian Crusaders who returned the fabled relic to the Realm. There, it has changed hands many times, eventually finding its way into the possession of one or more local noble families over the years.
Blood Bane

Beyond the shadow of a doubt, Saint Ambrosius was a devoted follower of the First Prophet. So devoted, some records say, that his attempts at caretaking nearly prevented the First Prophet from achieving his destiny of becoming a martyr. One very prominent tale, for example, comes from the First Prophet’s ill-fated trip to Gorguma. For preaching the gospel, the First Prophet was nearly stoned to death by an angry mob of pagans, but the city record of Gorguma stated he was saved in his eleventh hour by a madman of commendable size. That madman was in fact Saint Ambrosius, who flung himself headlong into the raucous mob with club in hand, ready to kill for his Prophet if need be.\\n\\nSaint Ambrosius is most famous for his stand upon Mount Ephlet, however. It was there, faced with a legion of Erebornian guardsmen searching for the First Prophet, that Saint Ambrosius rose – alone – to defend the son of his lord. Had it not been for a coward legionnaire’s cry for archers, Saint Ambrosius may well have fended off the Erebornians and thus prevented the crucifixion of the First Prophet. Were it not for thirty-three arrows, the “Lord’s Hound” as he was often called, might have single-handedly prevented the rise of the True Faith. Many believe his leather jerkin took the brunt of the archers’ assault, having been blessed by the Archangel Gabriel, who so admired Ambrosius’ unflinching will. After his death, the bloodied jerkin was removed and revered by the First Prophet’s followers as a holy relic... and a holey relic, too.
Saint Ambrosius's Skin

Though none can say for sure, consensus among church officials is that this relic was created at the request of the Praetorian Duke Giaccomo de Francovich. It was forged in the span of seven days by the smith Lammiel of Dansk, who was honored by the church in 991 for his piety. Giaccomo convinced poor Lammiel that he needed the shield for an ambitious campaign into Calmariland, where magic flows like water, when in truth, he intended to use the shield in a duel with the famous knight, Jean de René, whose wife Giaccomo had seduced. Giaccomo intended to blind his foe, rather than drain Calmarilandillish mages of their animus.\\n\\nAs Lammiel toiled on the seventh night, wet with sweat and proud beyond measure of the work he had done, he was met with a vision of the angel Raphael. Raphael, in his infinite wisdom, warned poor Lammiel that his shield would be used for ill, and Lammiel, straining against every fiber of his being, made a choice he oft-questioned. Lammiel, widely regarded as the greatest smith in Ultherst, intentionally flawed the shield he considered his greatest creation. Raphael blessed Lammiel and the shield for his sacrifice, turning it into an instrument of righteousness that only the purest of hearts could wield. When Giaccomo wore it into battle, he was felled – brutally – as was his traitor wife, driven mad by her lover’s death. Since, the shield has passed many hands, many of which fell behind the shield, too impure of heart to wield it safely. For that reason, and quite ironically, it has been called the “Liar’s Mirror” by some the vilest men to have ever lived.
Liar's Mirror

Though possessed of an almost angelic talent for smithing, Bonhart von Drichtmaul, the legendary blacksmith of Glatzburg, was unmatched in his inability to name weapons. In his time, he crafted two of some renown, both magnificent flails. He intended to use them to help beat back the barbarian hordes marching upon Ultherst in the mid-900s. This one, a smaller, one-handed variant of the other, he named simply “Lesser Morningstar.” Church historians claim both were enchanted by the angel Gabriel, who watched Von Drichtmaul as he worked. A shame, then, that the angel couldn’t have inspired a more worthy name.\\n\\n Though both of Von Drichtmaul’s weapons were forged to combat the barbarian invasion, they never tasted pagan blood. Both weapons fell into the hands of the enemy soon after their crafting, and were only retrieved during the barbarian’s final retreat in the year 989.
Lesser Morningstar

Various minstrel songs tell of the shield bestowed upon the First Knight, Mannfred, by the Archangel Michael atop Mount Agellion on the eve of the First Crusade. They say Mannfred was charged to carry the barrier in order to protect Wilhelm, his king, the chosen of the Lord and that he carried his burden graciously. The shield, owing in large part to its angelic creator, was wondrous to behold. It fulfilled its task at the Battle of Al-Quadim when Mannfred deflected three fatal blows directed at King Wilhelm. Unfortunately the shield could not save the life of its wielder, who was felled by an arrow to the back of the neck. After Mannfred’s death, the shield fell for a time into the hands of the Jad-Habaalian pagans. An Ultherstian noble by the name of Heidelbohn retrieved it before the end of the Crusades, and carried it with him back to the Realm. It remained in his family for generations, but was eventually lost. Now, somehow, it’s found its way here. Curious. Very curious.
Michael's Shield

Destroyer was the mighty axe of Vandor the Cruel, chieftain of the barbarian raiders who assaulted the Erebonian Empire in 395 of the Old Era. According to barbarian myths, the axe was forged by the semi-divine smiths Ethor and Unmair in the fabled city of Vallhard. There, barbarian gods and warrior kings waged war eternal between bouts of orgiastic feasting.\\n\\n Regardless of the veracity of ancient myths, the truth is wherever Vandor and Destroyer went, armies and cities fell. Even Bonorium, the Erebornian capital, eventually fell to the barbarian’s might. Vandor would later rename the empire Destroyer carved for him “Gubrinium.”\\n\\nAfter Vandor’s death, his two-bladed axe fell into the possession of Cleonus Flavius, a wandering merchant who brought it to his native city of Galibornium in the Filkland Peninsula. Destroyer remained in the Flavius family until the death of its last member, Honoricus Flavius, and was buried alongside him in the Flavius family tomb.
Destroyer

This stunningly beautiful ring was commissioned by Pope Dominicius when he assumed the Papal office in 1151. The ring soon became a symbol of the Holy Mother Church, owing the name “New Order” to Dominicius’ personal mission of reforming the church from within. During his reign, Pope Dominicius enacted a wide range of reforms that affected not only the Papal office but also the Archiepiscopal offices of every church in the faithful world. He made powerful enemies among the traditionalist faction of the Holy Mother Church, and thus, many of his reforms were redacted after his passing... but his magnificent ring lived on, passed from one pope to the next as a solemn reminder that the pope’s power, even bestowed by God, was ultimately limited by his fellow man.
New Order

This powerful necklace, known as The Eye of God, was created in the mid 12th century by Paolus I, the first pope in the history of the Holy Mother Church. Over the years, the Eye became one of the symbols of the Papal Cathedra—the office of the highest Patriarch. Anyone who draped the Eye around his neck was said to be able to resolve disputes calmly, deadening the emotions of anyone in the room as if the eyes of God were upon them. Paolus used the Eye to great effect during his reign, but with the coming of his successor, the artifact was relegated to the Papal treasury in favor of new artifacts. Eventually, the Eye fell into the possession of the Ultherstian Archbishop, Melanius, with whom it was eventually buried in a tomb not far from Alvaron.
Oculus Dei

According to the legends of people of Azthallaxu (a native kingdom of the New World), this ancient knife belonged to the god Guantharm who used it to kill the eternal snake, Onyx. From Onyx’s bowels, Guantharm created the Earth and sky. Although the legends are greatly exaggerated, the knife, “Onyx’s Bane” is in truth very ancient and very powerful. The famous conqueror, Raymond Flayerd, brought the weapon back to Calmariland with him after conquering the known New World. It was given, along with the rest of the treasures of Azthallax, to Carlos I, King of Calmariland. The treasure remained in Carlos’ possession until 1208, when pirates from the Island of Lost Souls pillaged the capitol. Onyx’s Bane, locked in the royal treasury, somehow vanished during the assault...
Onyx's Bane

Superstitious commoners have long scared their children with rumors of a “Girdle of Death” which was supposedly crafted in Kluthmorr, the most powerful stronghold of Dark Prophets in the whole of the Empire. Though Kluthmorr lies in ruins today, in the Old Era, it was a city of fantastic wealth and power where cultists the world over would congregate to worship the Cursed Flame and the Lord of Chaos. Given its dark past, Kluthmorr eventually became the Dark Prophet’s stronghold during the Hundred Years War. Cloaked in demon-skin robes, they dwelled in the dungeons below the ruins of Kluthmorr, from whence they hoped to spread their corruption to ever corner of the world. The last inhabitant of the dungeon was Lucius, a self-proclaimed Dark Prophet who was also proven to be the leader of the Children of the New Order.\\n\\n The Cult was discovered in 1019, and many of its supporters were arrested and executed soon after. Lucius himself was taken into custody only after Kluthmorr, then marked for destruction, fell to the Imperial army. The “Girdle of Death,” the symbol of Lucius’ unholy might, was not found on his person. Rumor has it that he secreted the belt away to prevent the church from taking possession of it. Its powers, to this day, remain a mystery...
Girdle of Death

By the time the Hundred Years War reached its climax, many of the world’s faithful kingdoms lay in ruin. Ravaged by war, these wayward kingdoms were ripe soil for those who sought to sow the seeds of heresy. Ultherst was no exception to that dark harvest.\\n\\n To combat the rising evil, the Inquisition enacted a law in 998 which gave sanctioned inquisitors the right to hunt and slay those who were suspected of heresy. A young inquisitorial priest by the name of Benedict of Ollm created a powerful magical staff during this time. He called it the Flame of Justice, naming it after a particularly violent psalm. In a terror-crazed rampage, Benedict of Ollm laid waste to several villages and townships in the Ultherstian countryside, fearing that the Hundred Years heresy had spread too deeply. Rather than putting Benedict down, the church declared him an Inquisitor General, and his wicked, ashen staff became a symbol of piety throughout the land.
Flame of Justice

Inquisitorial records dating back to the Hundred Years War claim the Fallen Archangel Azrael crafted this wicked stiletto from the bones of a tortured virgin girl. The weapon derives its name from the power Azrael imbued it wit; a single strike from the Devourer of Souls is supposedly enough to prevent an afflicted soul from passing on to the next plane of existence. These lost souls linger forever on the Earth, unable to ascend or descend after death. Instead, they seek to inhabit the dark weapon which trapped them.
Devourer of Souls

No Jad-Habaalian ruler inspired more fear and dread than Rafmani, the Man-Butcherm who once waged Holy War on the Erebornian Republic. In 385, he rallied a million-man army with the intent of eradicating the Erebornians, a goal the ruthless Sheikh might have reached if not for his blinding hubris.\\n\\n In the early days of Rafmani’s assault, his army of savages won several decisive victories, driving the Erebornians back - one loss at a time - to their lightly guarded capitol. At the Battle of Breth's Bridge, Rafmani’s men even succeeded in wiping out the entirety of the Republican Guard over the course of a few hours. The secret to Rafmani’s success was his sabre, the wicked Man Carver, which swam through men’s flesh like a fish through the sea. Forged from an unknown metal and imbued with spirits of the desert, the Man Carver served Rafmani well... until his strained army, pushed too far and stretched too thin, fell like a house of cards upon him.
Rafmani's Man Carver

Though the Orcs were a prolific race with a mind for war, they weren’t much for naming their weapons. This barbaric instrument, known only as “Rashgar’s Fist,” was said to have been able to shatter the bones of multiple foes with a single swing. Thought to be imbued with vast, demonic power, Rashgar’s Fist and the Orc who wielded it terrorized townships near the Moonshine Mountains for centuries. Funny. Without Rashgar, wouldn’t it just be called “Fist”?
Rashgar's Fist

Any wayward soul who’s ever felt the sting of a sheriff’s lash or the heel or a soldier’s boot surely knows the story of King David of Lochland. David, born an Erebornian noble’s son, climbed from a place of relative obscurity to great heights within the Empire, only to then trade the Emperor’s glory for God’s. Fitting, for it was David, garbed in the rags of a commoner, who slew Emperor Constantine in a duel on the steps of the Imperial Palace.\\n\\n David, like most Erebornian nobles, lived a life of wild luxury and excess. His father, Patriarch Desdemonus Heraclius, was an influential senator and one of the richest men in Ereborn, and his mother, daughter of a local lord, knew only the pampered life of high-blooded marrying-stock. David was a cruel boy by nature, shaped no doubt by his father’s wicked cunning. He changed his ways only after meeting Saint Sebestian, who first taught the young noble the path of God. The martyr's eventual death left a great impact on the young, would-be king. So much so that he sought to change his very destiny.\\n\\n Mourning the loss of his friend and mentor Sebestian, David surrendered all of his worldly possessions and made a pilgrimage to the Sinmar Mountain to live the life of a hermit. There he stayed in the company of Saint Dominicus, who baptized the young pagan in the name of the Lord.\\n\\nWhen the Erebornian rebellion erupted in in 219, David returned to his hometown of Haelesmar to help to overthrow the ruling tyrant, a vile and heartless pagan monster. That tyrant’s blood was the water which would nurture the tree of young David’s righteousness. Gifted with his father’s charisma and strategic skills, David soon made himself a leader of men.\\n\\n In 223, David marched a grand army to Bonorium, the capitol of Ereborn. It was there that he accepted the crown of the newly founded Lochland Kingdom from the hands of the Bishop of Bonorium. Enraged by his Bishop’s betrayal, and incensed that an upstart boy from a newfound religion would ever dare to challenge him, the Emperor Constantine met young David in a duel at the Imperial Palace. It lasted for hours, David deflecting blow after blow from the wild Emperor with his favored wood-cutting axe, and the Emperor, furious beyond consoling, swinging his broadsword with reckless abandon. When at last the sun drew low in the sky and the Emperor’s spirits were beginning to run low, David made his move. He took Constantine’s head with a swing of his axe, and severed a man and a nation in one fell swoop. Some say David’s axe, to this day, still possesses the power to shatter Empires.
King David's Axe

Orc’s Bane was the fabled axe of King Harlior, ruler of the sub-human Thron Empire, deep below the Moonshine Mountain range. Harlior fought the Orcs, who sought to steal his kingdom, tooth and nail. He finally fell in a duel with Khan Rashgar, Lord of the Orcs, who slew the great king with a blow from his mighty hammer. After his death, neither the king’s body nor his magnificent axe were ever found, leading many to believe he would rise from the Netherworld to reclaim his kingdom one day.\\n\\n Orc’s Bane is made of the finest steel, the crafting of which was lost with the fall of Thron. Legends say King Harlior could severed the heads of several Orcs in a single swing; For the Orc’s sake, let’s pray those legends were true.
Orc’s Bane

No weapon is more storied among the Brotherhood of the Righteous than the Lord’s Sword, “Decapitator.” According to the Brotherhood’s records, Commander Giordano de Loisson forged it in 1120 on the eve of  an assault on the headquarters of the Blood Moon cult. The cult, founded by a band of fallen crusaders, centered itself around the worship of a tainted Jad-Habaalian blade. In mad fits of rage, the Blood Moon cultists would steal into towns and villages, slitting throats and severing limbs for the glory of a foreign blade and the Brothers, outraged to see their comrades lost to the throes of madness, vowed to see justice done.\\n\\n When at last the Brothers found the cult’s hideout and trailed its followers into the sewers beneath Alvaron, the Blood Moons put up a truly legendary fight. Many stories were written of the battle, which reportedly lasted for hours. Brothers falling to poisoned blades, cultists falling before the might of Commander De Loisson’s righteous blade – the carnage was truly magnificent in its scope.\\n\\n According to legend, when the last cultist fell, his last, pained breath was spent begging for mercy. The Commander, and every commander who’s wielded the blade since, answered the enemy’s plea for mercy with wordless grace. It doesn’t take a scholar to find out how Decapitator earned its name...
Decapitator

This weapon, likely made during the barbarian occupation, bears the inscription “Brave Heart.” The name, as the blade, carries more than a little history.\\n\\ Near the end of the occupation, King Hermann III fled into the Moonshine Mountains with the last of his retinue, scrounging for food in hopes of someday raising a foreign army. One misty morning, as the sun rose over the jagged peaks of Moonshine, a lone warrior wandered up the path—eventually he and Saint Jilliam would start the uprising at Drachtbaum, the death knell of the Barbarian occupation. His name was Elmer of Glen Coil, and a look into his terribly cold eyes was often enough to send the foreign dogs skittering for the hills.\\n\\n Though Elmer was a terror in his own right, much of the fear associated with his name was, to a great degree, brought about by his massive two-handed sword, “Brave Heart.” Church rumors say the blade was blessed by Saint Jillian with water from the river Sanctus, though how the saint might have come by waters from that river so far in the mountains, none could say.\\n\\n After the uprising at Drachtbaum, Elmer became the First Knight of King Hermann III and Brave Heart, his mighty weapon, became the symbol of his office. To this day, it remains so.
Brave Heart

King David, the boy king who killed an Emperor, was the first ruler of Lochland. His journey from soldier to King was long and arduous, and along the way, he made many friends and many enemies.
